title_original: Discovering John Baer, an Untrained Master Photographer
excerpt_original: He acquired a camera from a captured German soldier in 1945 and went on to shoot some of the best postwar Europe and New York City street photographs you’ve never seen.

blocks.text: On a recent Saturday at The White Loft, a gallery on the Lower East Side, Andrew Baer showed me a 1938 Leica Model III. His father, John Baer, acquired the camera from a captured German soldier in 1945 while he was deployed to Germany in World War II. He took his first shots in Wetzlar, home of the Leica headquarters, where he happened to be stationed. What followed was a decade of obsessive picture-taking, a quotidian quest through post-war Europe and midcentury New York, the wondrous results of which remained largely unknown until 2021. These photographs sat untouched for decades, until John died in 1994 and Andrew discovered three boxes in a damp corner of his father’s basement.

A selection of black-and-white images, hanging unframed on the Loft’s walls, showed what he discovered — a series of Baer’s experiments in looking. In Europe, he captured people among the ruins of war; in New York, he studied shadows on Stuyvesant Town, asphalt pavers engulfed in smoke, intimate moments between friends in Bryant Park, street scenes taken from the fire escape of his fifth-floor walkup on Second Avenue in the East Village. The first image I noticed, “Rainy Day Reflections,” showed a slice of sunlight stretching across Lexington Avenue, a pedestrian caught midstride, whose umbrella mimics the manhole cover.
